title: A Rule You Can Say
bigQuestion: Why does a short written rule help strangers play the same game?

story.title: Two Classes, One Line
story.kicker: Children from two classes meet at a painted line and both know what it means.
paragraphs: Recess. A second-grade line and a third-grade line reach the same white paint. No one planned a meeting. The line was already there on the blacktop.
A teacher says to stay behind the line until the whistle. Both classes hear the same sentence. The game can start without a long speech from anyone.
That sentence is a rule you can say. It is short. A child can repeat it. Strangers do not need a private code to begin. That is the point.
Sports leagues print longer books. The idea is the same as the painted line: say the rule so two towns can play one game.
story.think: What is one short rule you can say about a game at your school?

lessons.title: A Sentence Everyone Can Repeat
lessons.mainIdea: A useful playground rule is a short sentence children can say aloud.
reading: A good start rule is short. Stay behind the line until the whistle is one sentence. Children can repeat it to a friend.
Long secret codes do not travel. A short sentence travels from one class to the next class at recess.

words.d: words that tell how a game will be shared

look.title: Say it once
look.text: A teacher holds up one finger and says one sentence. Twenty children say it back. The line does not move. The words do the work.
look.prompt: Why might one sentence work better than a long speech at recess?

check.q: What makes a playground start rule useful?
choices: it is a short sentence children can say
it is written only in Latin

check.q: What happens to long secret codes?
Who can repeat a short rule?
check.why: Children can repeat a short sentence.

lessons.title: Lines Help Strangers
lessons.mainIdea: A painted line is a rule you can see, so people who just met can start together.
reading: A *line* on blacktop or grass is paint. It is also a rule. Stay behind it. Start on it. Do not cross it yet.
Two children who have never met can both use that line. They do not need to be friends first. The paint does the introducing.

words.d: a painted mark that shows where to stand or start

look.title: Paint as a sentence
look.text: Look at a white line on blacktop. No words are printed on it. Still, both classes treat it as wait here. The mark stands in for a sentence.
look.prompt: What sentence is the line saying?

check.q: What is a painted line in this lesson?
check.why: The line is a visible rule.

check.q: Do children need to be friends first to use the line?
choices: no, the paint works for strangers
check.why: Strangers can share a painted line.
The reading says the paint introduces the rule.

lessons.title: The Laws of the Game
lessons.mainIdea: Soccer's Laws of the Game are a printed book so clubs in many countries can use the same rules.
reading: The International Football Association Board, or IFAB, writes the *Laws of the Game*. Those laws are the world rule book for soccer.
A club in one country and a club in another country can play if they both use that book. The book does what the playground line does, at a larger size.

words.d: the official world rule book for soccer, written by IFAB

look.title: One book for many countries
look.text: IFAB publishes the Laws of the Game so matches in different countries can use the same numbered laws, including Law 3 on how many players and Law 5 on the referee.
look.cite: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 3 and Law 5
look.prompt: What problem does one world book try to solve?

check.q: Who writes the Laws of the Game?
Why print the laws in a book?
choices: so clubs in many countries can use the same rules
check.why: A shared book lets distant clubs play.

lessons.title: 1863 Was a Meeting About Words
lessons.mainIdea: The Football Association met in London in 1863 to write one set of kicking rules.
reading: On 26 October 1863, clubs met in London. They formed the Football Association. They wanted one written game, not a different game on every green.
That meeting was about words on paper. The pitch came with the words. Without shared words, the rectangle would not mean the same thing in two towns.

words.d: the group formed in London in 1863 to write shared soccer rules

look.title: Freemasons' Tavern
look.text: The Football Association's first meeting was at the Freemasons' Tavern in London on 26 October 1863. The clubs came to agree on written rules for the kicking game.
look.cite: The Football Association, founding meeting, 26 October 1863
look.prompt: What did the clubs come to agree on?

check.q: When did the Football Association first meet?

choices: a different game on every green

check.why: It was a meeting about written rules.

lessons.title: IHSA Handbooks
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois high schools use IHSA by-laws and sport terms so state series can be fair.
reading: The IHSA publishes by-laws and sport terms. Schools that join agree to those words. That is how a school in Cairo and a school in Rockford can meet.
The handbook is not a playbook. It does not teach a formation. It says who may play and how a state series is run.

words.d: the written rules a school agrees to when it joins the IHSA

look.title: One state, one handbook
look.text: IHSA member schools follow the association's by-laws and the terms for each sport so regional and state series use the same eligibility and meet rules.
look.cite: Illinois High School Association Constitution and By-Laws
look.prompt: Why must Cairo and Rockford use the same handbook?

check.q: What do IHSA schools agree to follow?

choices: how a state series is run

check.q: Cairo and Rockford can meet because
check.why: Shared IHSA words make a state series possible.

lessons.title: A Referee Carries a Book
lessons.mainIdea: By the late 1800s a soccer referee used a written law book, not only a spoken custom.
reading: Soccer's Laws of the Game gave the referee a written job. The referee starts play, stops play, and carries the laws onto the pitch.
IFAB still writes those laws. A referee in two countries can open the same numbered book.

words.d: the official who starts and stops a soccer match
the board that writes the Laws of the Game

look.title: Law 5
look.text: IFAB Law 5 says the referee enforces the Laws of the Game and may use a whistle so everyone hears the same decision.
look.cite: IFAB, Laws of the Game, Law 5 (The Referee)
look.prompt: Why does the referee carry a book and a whistle?

choices: the written laws onto the pitch
check.why: The laws go onto the field.

choices: a short sentence children can say
